# Methods

We did a cluster-randomised trial in 48 primary care clinics in two provinces between March 1, 2019, and Feb 28, 2021. Clinics were eligible if they diagnosed at least 20 people with tuberculosis each year. The primary outcome was treatment success at 12 months, defined as cure or completion without evidence of failure. We estimated the risk ratio with a log-binomial model that accounted for clustering, and we used multiple imputation for the 6% of participants with missing outcomes.

# Results

Of 3812 people screened, 2945 were enrolled: 1478 in intervention clinics and 1467 in control clinics (figure 1). Treatment success was 86·2% in intervention clinics and 79·5% in control clinics (risk ratio 1·08, 95% CI 1·03–1·14; p=0·0021). The effect was similar in people with and without HIV (appendix p 6).

# Discussion

In this trial, adherence support delivered by community health workers increased treatment success by 6·7 percentage points. Two earlier trials in Peru and South Africa reported smaller differences, probably because their control clinics already offered home visits. Our study has several limitations. First, outcomes were taken from routine registers, which might have missed deaths after transfer; this would bias the estimate towards the null. Second, clinics were not masked to allocation.
